newsitem.title: PAKISTAN: World Bank official to lead Pakistan's economy.
newsitem.headline: World Bank official to lead Pakistan's economy.

text.p: World Bank Vice-President Javed Burki will take charge of Pakistan's Finance Ministry under the newly appointed caretaker government, a senior government official said on Thursday.

Burki, a Pakistani national, will be adviser to the ministry but in charge of finance, economic affairs and planning, the official told Reuters, speaking anonymously. There will be no finance minister in the caretaker cabinet, he said.
"He (Burki) is going to join the government," the official said. "He will be adviser for finance, economic affairs and planning, and be effectively in charge of these divisions of the government."
Burki would take temporary leave from his post at the Washington-based bank. But under World Bank rules, he could not accept the finance minister position, the official said.

He said there was no need for a finance minister in the interim government, which took office on Tuesday after former prime minister Benazir Bhutto's government was dismissed. General elections are set for February 3, 1997.
Burki sharply criticised Bhutto's government in a recent series of interviews and articles in which he analysed what he called a dozen "faultlines" in Pakistan's economy.

"A faultline can cause tremors; it can also cause great damage," he wrote in one article. "It represents a deep structural flaw against which the structures that are built on top must be robust and properly reinforced."
Bhutto reacted irately, with newspapers quoting her in mid-September as denouncing "some World Bank officials in Washington" for creating problems for her government.

Pakistan is saddled with burdensome external debt, weak industrial growth and inflation, said Sartaj Aziz, who was finance minister in a former government led by the current opposition leader Nawaz Sharif.
On Wednesday, Moody's Investors Service lowered Pakistan's sovereign ceiling foreign-currency debt rating to B2 from B1.

The New York-based credit rating agency said the downgrade reflected "the increased fragility of Pakistan's liquidity position and the severe pressures that the large domestic and foreign currency debt burden exert on public finances, the external accounts and official reserves".

Pakistan is negotiating an agreement with the International Monetary Fund over a stalled $600 million standby loan seen as crucial for shoring up the nation's finances. The talks continued this week despite the abrupt change of government.
Moody's said the IMF and other multilateral and bilateral creditors were expected to resume disbursements of agreed loans within the next month.
